P3609 Introductory note to 1936a
P3610 In this abstract, published in Lirgebnisse emes mathematischen Kolloquiums, Godel announced a “speed-up” theorem that holds when one switches from a weaker logic to a stronger one. (The term “logic” may be somewhat misleading since apparatus for proving facts about numbers is, of course, present.) Godel had already shown that a logic Sn+1 of a higher order could prove formulas that a logic S,, of a lower order could not prove. Now he considered the question of formulas that can be proved in both the weaker and the stronger logics, and his theo rem stated that, if the length of a proof is defined to be the number of lines in it, there are formulas that can be proved in both S,, and Sy41 but that have a proof in S,4, much shorter than their shortest proof in S,. Thus S,41 achieves a speed-up over S,,. This speed-up can be by an arbitrary function computable in S,, in the sense that, for any function ¢ computable in S,,, there would be a formula A and a number & such that A can be proved in S,41 in & lines but, although provable in S, also, A cannot be proved in S, in $(k) lines.
P3611 The notion of computability in a formal system that is used here is what Godel had previously called Entscheidungsdefinitheit in 1981. In terestingly, Godel did not remark at first that the notion of computable function in S, is independent of n, but this crucial observation was added in the page proof before publication. Gédel later remarked, in the first paragraph of his paper 1946, that his notion of computability in a logic is equivalent to Turing computability, and he stressed that this is an absolute notion independent of the formalism chosen. Incidentally, it is worth mentioning here that Gédel does not bother to make a dis tinction between a function ¢ and the syntactic object corresponding to its representation in S,. It is true of course, by virtue of Gédel’s own incompleteness results, that two different representations of the same function may fail to be provably equivalent.
P3612 Godel did not give a proof of his result, but an analogous result taking the length of a proof to be its Gédel number, rather than the number of lines in it, was given by Mostowski in 1952. Similar results were also proved by Ehrenfeucht and Mycielski (4971) and by Parikh (1971). The case where n > 1 is not explicitly stated by these authors, but Solomon 1981 gives an argument based on some complexity-theoretic results of Hartmanis 1978.
P3613 4See Davis 1982, pp. 15-16, for a discussion, as well as pp. 340-342 of the intro ductory note to 1934 in this volume.
P3614 The case where the length of proof is measured by the number of lines appears to be open for n > 1. Thus, in the following, we shall consider only the case where S, is replaced by some version PA of Peano arith metic, and S,41 by some system S in which the consistency of Peano arithmetic is provable.
P3615 A crucial difference between taking the length of a proof to be the number of lines and taking it to be its Godel number (equivalently, the number of symbols) is that there are infinitely many proofs with a given number of lines, but only finitely many with a given number of symbols. This affects both the character of the demonstration and the impact of the result. For example, a result formulated in terms of Gédel numbers tends to apply also to arbitrary recursive axiomatizations of PA and S. However, it is easy to find recursive axiomatizations of any recursively enumerable theory (PA in particular) so that all theorems have proofs of only three lines at most. Thus a result proved in terms of the length of a proof as the number of lines must make essential use of the fact that the usual formalizations of familiar systems are schematic in nature; all axioms and rules fall under a finite number of schemata.
P3616 Returning to Gédel’s work, we note that there is some ambiguity about the precise result being claimed. Namely, it is not obvious from the abstract whether Gédel intended + and x to be function symbols or predicate symbols in his logics. A remark at the beginning of Section 2 of his 1991 seems to indicate that it might be the latter.
P3617 This point is of some importance. While systems formalized using function or predicate symbols respectively for the same objects have the same proof-theoretic strength, the proofs tend to be shorter with the former. For instance, the formula t = t, where ¢ is a complicated term, can be an axiom if function symbols are available, but must be stated (and proved) in a roundabout way in terms of predicate symbols if that is all we have. (Gédel does not remark on this last fact.) It was shown in Parikh 1978 that, if PA* is the version of PA where + and x are ternary predicate symbols, then there are sequences A; of formulas whose proofs in S are uniformly bounded in length but whose proofs in PA* must be unbounded in length. Gédel’s theorem for n = 1 follows as a corollary, and we can eliminate the requirement that the speed-up be by a com putable function.
P3618 The argument of Parikh 1978 depended on showing that the question “Does a given formula have a proof in PA* of k lines or less?” is decid able. While the corresponding question for the usual formalization of PA is open, a recent result by Goldfarb (1981) seems to indicate that a positive result is unlikely. However, Statman (1981) showed that when a theory T, axiomatized with a finite number of schemata, is extended by adding an undecidable formula A, and TU{-A} has an infinite model,
P3619 then even tautologies become easier to prove. The Gédel theorem for n = 1 follows immediately.
P3620 A general study of the speed-up phenomenon in the context of proofs appears in Statman 1978. The term “speed-up” is not due to Gédel but was introduced by Blum (1967) in the context of complexity the ory. Subsequently, the phenomenon of speed-up became a major topic

P3648 It can, moreover, be shown that a function computable in one of the sys tems S;, or even in a system of transfinite order, is computable already in S;. P3654 (3) the variable-binding operation “Az”, which generates from an expres sion with the free variable z the function defined by it. This system, on the one hand, can still be proved consistent by finitary means and, on the other, is so comprehensive that every number-theoretic function defined by recursion (of arbitrarily high order) is contained in it; that is, for every such function ¢ there is a formula F of the system such that, ifn is an arbitrary natural number and m = ¢(n), the formula F(n) = m is provable, where the natural numbers 1,2,3,... and so on are represented by the following formulas: Afa - f(x), Afx- f(f(x)), Afx- f(f(f(x))),... and so on (see Godel 1984e). The numbers | and 2 are at the same time employed as the truth values “false” and “true”, and the operations of the propositional calculus are introduced by definition as number-theoretic functions. The formula 2 is the sole axiom, and all the rules of inference (which the author calls “conversions” ) are reversible, so that a formula is regarded as proved if it can be converted into 2. The universal quantifier does not appear as a primitive notion but is represented by certain formulas II, built up by means of the three primitive notions, having the property that II(F,G) is provable if and only if G(x) can be derived from F(z) by means of certain rules of inference differing in general from the conversions. In consequence of the fact that every formal system is incomplete, a transfinite sequence of ever stronger rules of inference, and correspondingly a transfinite sequence of different universal quantifiers, can be defined. It is conjectured that these correspond to the different orders of proof by mathematical induction.

P3660 Concerning our translations, a few points should be mentioned. In 19892 Godel uses “Zahlausdruck”, borrowed from Léwenheim, and in 1929 he uses “Zahlaxiomsystem”. For him, the first expression refers to a closed well-formed formula of first-order logic, and the second to an applied (in the sense of Church) first-order axiom system. Various names are used by GéGdel and others for first-order logic: “restricted functional calculus” (or, in German, “engerer Funktionenkalkiil”, used by Hilbert and Acker mann), “first-order predicate calculus” (or simply “predicate calculus”), “quantification theory” (used by Quine), and perhaps others. The editors have not imposed uniformity here, and the reader should be aware of this diversity. Gédel’s “Funktionenvariable” has been translated as “functional variable” and refers to what is now commonly known as a predicate letter. At times Stefan Bauer-Mengelberg’s neologism “contentual” has been used to translate “inhaltlich” .
P3661 When used with function names that have superscripts, like f7", the prime notation introduced on page 90 becomes ambiguous, and we have inserted parentheses to mark the scope: (f7”)’. Moreover, in Gédel’s text up to the end of Section 6, the superscript m was, at some occurrences, mistakenly interchanged with the subscript l.

Footnote 16 now consists of the last part of item 9, the first part having been incorporated into the 1965 text. Footnote 2, incorporating item 1 of the “Notes and errata”, was modified in the 1965 text to begin “This sentence could have been”; but we have retained the original wording of item 1: “This sentence may be”. Finally, in 1965 the text and footnotes originally on page 28 became what is now the last paragraph of Section 8, and the text itself was amplified.
